remote_covid.note: Neither mentions remote work or COVID-19.

data_window.note: Not stated by either; period of the ~300-company analysis not given.

cat_productivity.note: Productivity gains (16–30% top performers; 40–70% and 50% in cases; 10x/20x), used in aggregate without operational definition.

cat_quality.note: Software quality gains (31–45%); defect rates as a tracked outcome.

cat_collaboration.note: Human review of agent output appears as a skill, not a collaboration measure.

cat_satisfaction.note: Only customer experience, not developer satisfaction.

cat_delivery.note: Time to market (16–30%), release frequency as tracked outcome, idea-to-impact cycle time.

cat_agile.note: NotebookLM lists the shift from two-week sprints to daily sprint reviews as a delivery-cadence metric; Claude mentions the daily sprint review only in the narrative.

cat_survey.note: Method of the ~300-company analysis not described; no perceptual instrument.

evidence.quote: Excerpted with permission from the publisher, Wiley, from Rewired: How Leading Companies Win with Technology and AI by Eric Lamarre, Kate Smaje, and Rob Levin, with Alex Singla and Alexander Sukharevsky.
If gen AI has a killer application, it’s software development—one of the most profound shifts in the history of programming.

We found that a small group of top performers—roughly the top quintile—are achieving 16–30 percent improvements in productivity, time to market, and customer experience, along with 31–45 percent gains in software quality.
